title: "I will not rise"
hook: he resolves not to move until he awakens

segments.voice: Yesterday, eight handfuls of grass: a gift from a grass-cutter, spread as a seat facing east. Your line was a seat is a decision. Where did you sit on purpose? Day fifty-one.
screen: `EIGHT HANDFULS OF GRASS — A SEAT IS A DECISION.`

segments.voice: A workout you'll quit if it gets too hard. A writing session with the phone face-up beside you. Ten minutes of meditation, and at minute four a voice says, you know, that's probably enough. An exit built into everything can feel safe. It also means never finding out what's on the other side of staying. The wanderer is sitting on his seat of grass under the great fig tree, facing east. The sun is going down. And before the night begins, he makes a vow. Today's word is what he vowed to find.
screen: `AN EXIT BUILT INTO EVERYTHING.` → `AT MINUTE FOUR...` → `A VOW AT SUNSET.`

segments.voice: The later telling gives the vow in dramatic words. Let my skin and sinews and bones dry up. Let the flesh and blood in my body wither. But I will not rise from this seat until I have found complete awakening. It sounds like the old austerities, but it isn't. He's not starving now; he's eaten. He's not forcing his breath. He's just decided not to leave. The difference between forcing and staying is the whole lesson of the last two weeks. The Pali canon has a similar resolve in the Buddha's own words: let only skin and sinews and bones remain, but my effort will not slacken until I reach what can be reached. And the thing he's staying for has a name: bodhi. It means awakening. It comes from a root, budh, that means to wake up, to become aware, to understand. The same root is in the word Buddha, which we'll get to soon. In Buddhist teaching, bodhi is not a trance, or a vision, or a feeling of bliss. It's pictured as waking up, the way you wake from a dream and see the room as it actually is. That's why the tree became the Bodhi tree, and the place Bodh Gaya. The word stuck to everything around that night. Staying put, in Buddhist practice, doesn't mean gritting your teeth through pain. It means not running. When restlessness says get up, you notice it, and stay. When boredom says check your phone, you notice it, and stay. The noticing is the practice.
screen: `I WILL NOT RISE FROM THIS SEAT.` · `NOT FORCING. STAYING.` · `BODHI — FROM BUDH, TO WAKE UP.` · `STAYING PUT IS NOT RUNNING.` · then, large: `STAY PUT.`

segments.voice: Sit on your seat. Before the bell, make a small vow, the size of today: for these two minutes, I'll stay. Not perfectly still, not perfectly calm. Just here. Then sit. When the mind says that's enough, notice it, and stay. When an itch comes, notice it, and see if it passes. When a thought pulls you away, come back to the breath. You're not fighting anything. You're just not leaving. The bell holds the time.
Bodhi. Awakening, from the root budh, to wake up. What the wanderer vowed not to rise without, and the name of the tree he sat beneath.
Your line: stay put. Today, choose one thing, five minutes of work, a conversation, a sit, and do it fully, without an exit. Day fifty-one.

howItsDone: Some Buddhist meditators begin a sit or a retreat by making a quiet resolve (adhitthana) to stay for a set time, and resolve is counted among the perfections in Theravada teaching.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit: awakening, from the root budh, to wake up, to know.

trapdoor: what you thought: bodhi is the name of a tree.
what it means: bodhi is awakening itself. the tree was named for what happened beneath it.
what a scholar hears: bodhi, from budh (to wake, to perceive); the resolve (skin, sinews and bones) appears in the canon, e.g. MN 70 and AN 2.5, and in the Nidanakatha at the Bodhi tree.
